Topic 1: Prosperity, Inequality, and Planetary Limits **Course Alignment**: *CORE Microeconomics 2.0* Ch. 1.1–1.6, Extension 1.2, 1.8–1.9, 1.13 | **Lectures 1–2** (Whiteboard 1) | **Exercises Topic 1** ### 1.1 Measuring Income, Inequality, and Growth #### Rich/Poor Ratio (90/10 Ratio) To measure inequality within a country, *CORE* orders the population from poorest to richest, divides it into ten equal groups (**deciles**, each holding $10\%$ of the population), and defines the **rich/poor ratio** as: $$\text{Rich/poor ratio} = \frac{\text{Average income of the richest } 10\% \text{ (Decile 10)}}{\text{Average income of the poorest } 10\% \text{ (Decile 1)}}$$ *(Note: Notice that this is the ratio of the **average** incomes of the top and bottom deciles, unlike the 90/10 percentile ratio which compares the single individual at the 90th percentile to the 10th percentile. In Spring 2025 Exam Part 1 Q1, a rich/poor ratio of $85$ means the average income of the richest $10\%$ is $85$ times that of the poorest $10\%$.)* - **Key Mathematical Properties (Topic 1 Exercise 1)**: Let $I_{\text{top}} > I_{\text{bottom}} > 0$ be the average incomes of the top $10\%$ and bottom $10\%$: 1. **Equal Percentage Growth Leaves the Ratio Unchanged**: If both groups' incomes increase by the same percentage $g$ (e.g., $+50\%$, multiplying both by $1 + g = 1.5$), the multiplier cancels out: $$\frac{(1 + g)I_{\text{top}}}{(1 + g)I_{\text{bottom}}} = \frac{I_{\text{top}}}{I_{\text{bottom}}}$$ *(Example: If $I_{\text{top}} = 1,000,000\text{ NOK}$ and $I_{\text{bottom}} = 100,000\text{ NOK}$, the initial ratio is $10$. A $50\%$ increase raises them to $1,500,000$ and $150,000$; the ratio is still $10$, even though the absolute gap grew from $900,000$ to $1,350,000\text{ NOK}$.)* 2. **Equal Absolute (NOK) Addition Reduces the Ratio**: If both groups receive the same fixed amount $\Delta > 0$ (e.g., $+50,000\text{ NOK}$), this represents a larger percentage gain for the poorest decile than for the richest decile, so the ratio **falls** toward $1$: $$\frac{I_{\text{top}} + \Delta}{I_{\text{bottom}} + \Delta} < \frac{I_{\text{top}}}{I_{\text{bottom}}} \quad \text{whenever } I_{\text{top}} > I_{\text{bottom}} \text{ and } \Delta > 0$$ *(With $\Delta = 50,000\text{ NOK}$, the new ratio is $1,050,000 / 150,000 = 7 < 10$.)* #### GDP per Capita, PPP, and Ratio Scales - **Gross Domestic Product (GDP) per capita**: Total market value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a year divided by total population. It measures average annual output (value creation) per person. - **Constant Prices (Real GDP) & Purchasing Power Parity (PPP)**: - **Constant prices** adjust nominal GDP for inflation over time by valuing output at the prices of a fixed base year. - **PPP (Purchasing Power Parity)** adjusts for price differences across countries by valuing output using a common set of international prices, so $\$1$ of PPP GDP buys the same basket of goods in Norway, India, or the US. - **Linear Scale vs. Ratio (Logarithmic) Scale (Lecture 1 & Whiteboard 1)**: - On a **linear vertical axis**, equal vertical distances represent equal *absolute* additions (e.g., $+10,000\text{ USD}$). Long-run GDP per capita looks like a flat line for a thousand years followed by an abrupt vertical "hockey stick" kink after 1800. - On a **ratio scale** (where the vertical axis doubles at each tick mark: $500 \to 1,000 \to 2,000 \to 4,000 \to 8,000$), equal vertical distances represent equal **percentage growth rates**. - **Visual Rule for Ratio Scales**: - A **straight upward-sloping line** on a ratio scale means the **annual percentage growth rate is constant**. - A **steeper line** means a **higher percentage growth rate**; a **flatter line** means a **lower percentage growth rate**. --- ### 1.2 Production Functions and Diminishing Average Product #### Total Output, Average Product ($APL$), and Marginal Product ($MPL$) In agricultural and Malthusian economies (as well as short-run firm production with fixed capital/land), output $Y$ (e.g., grain in kg) is produced using variable labour $L$ (number of farmers) on a fixed quantity of land: $$Y = f(L)$$ | Concept | Symbol & Formula | Geometric Interpretation on $Y = f(L)$ Graph | Economic Meaning | | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Total Product** | $Y = f(L)$ | Height of the production function curve at input $L$. | Total output produced by $L$ workers on fixed land. | | **Average Product of Labour ($APL$)** | $APL(L) = \frac{Y}{L} = \frac{f(L)}{L}$ | **Slope of the ray from the origin $(0,0)$** to the point $(L, Y)$ on the curve. | Average output produced per worker. | | **Marginal Product of Labour ($MPL$)** | $MPL(L) = \frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta L} \approx \frac{df(L)}{dL}$ | **Slope of the tangent line** to the production function at point $(L, Y)$. | Additional output produced by employing one more worker, holding land/capital fixed. | #### Diminishing Average Product of Labour & the Malthusian Trap - **Why $APL$ Diminishes**: When more farmers work on a **fixed quantity of land** (or when more inferior land must be brought into cultivation), each farmer has less land to work with. Because the production function $Y = f(L)$ is **strictly concave** ($f'(L) > 0, f''(L) < 0$): 1. Each additional worker adds less to total output than the previous worker (**diminishing marginal product**, $MPL$ is decreasing). 2. For every $L > 0$, the tangent slope is flatter than the ray from the origin ($MPL(L) < APL(L)$). Because the marginal worker produces less than the current average, adding workers **pulls the average product $APL(L)$ down**. - **Worked Numerical Verification (Topic 1 Exercise 3 & Lecture 2)**: - At **Point A**: $L_A = 800\text{ farmers}$ produce $Y_A = 500,000\text{ kg}$ of grain: $$APL_A = \frac{500,000\text{ kg}}{800\text{ farmers}} = \mathbf{625\text{ kg per farmer}}$$ - At **Point B**: Doubling labour to $L_B = 1,600\text{ farmers}$ increases total grain output less than proportionally to $Y_B = 778,000\text{ kg}$: $$APL_B = \frac{778,000\text{ kg}}{1,600\text{ farmers}} = \mathbf{486.25\text{ kg per farmer}} < 625\text{ kg per farmer}$$ - Across the interval from $800$ to $1,600$ farmers, the average marginal product is $\frac{\Delta Y}{\Delta L} = \frac{778,000 - 500,000}{1,600 - 800} = \frac{278,000}{800} = \mathbf{347.5\text{ kg per additional farmer}}$. ![Total output production function with rays from origin and diminishing APL/MPL curves](./static-data/vault-assets/EXC3420-Obsidian/EXC3420-support/assets/01-production-function.svg) *Figure 1.1: (a) Grain production function $Y=f(L)$ from Topic 1 Exercise 3 showing that the ray from the origin to $B(1600, 778\text{k})$ is flatter than the ray to $A(800, 500\text{k})$, and the tangent at $A$ ($MPL$) is flatter than the ray to $A$ ($APL$). (b) Because $MPL < APL$ everywhere, $APL$ slopes downward from $625\text{ kg}$ at $L=800$ to $486.25\text{ kg}$ at $L=1600$.* > [!warning] Common Exam Trap: Diminishing $APL$ Does NOT Mean Total Output Falls! > In multiple-choice questions (e.g., *Spring 2025 Part 1 Q3* and *V2026 Part 1 Q1*), students often confuse **diminishing average/marginal product** with **falling total output**. As $L$ rises from $800$ to $1,600$, **total output increases** from $500,000\text{ kg}$ to $778,000\text{ kg}$ ($MPL > 0$), while **output per farmer ($APL$) decreases** from $625\text{ kg}$ to $486.25\text{ kg}$. --- ### 1.3 Capitalism, Specialization, and Planetary Limits #### The Three Pillars of Capitalism (*CORE* Ch. 1.8 & Lectures 1–2) In economic analysis, **capitalism** is not a single institution but an **economic system** defined by the combination of three distinct institutions: 1. **Private Property**: The right to use, exclude others from, and transfer ownership of possessions—most importantly **capital goods** (equipment, buildings, patented technology, and raw materials used in production). *(Exam staple: Public goods and natural views like **the view from Mount Ulriken** [Spring 2024 Q1] or **national security** [Fall 2024 Q4] are **not** covered by private property rights; nor is human labour under non-slave law).* 2. **Markets**: Means of transferring goods and services that are **reciprocal** (unlike gifts or theft), **voluntary** (both buyer and seller participate only if the exchange improves their wellbeing), and typically subject to **competition**. 3. **Capitalist Firms**: Business organizations owned by private individuals that **(a)** own or rent capital goods, **(b)** hire workers for wages (creating a **labour market**), and **(c)** sell goods and services on markets with the goal of **making a profit**. #### Gains from Specialization and Division of Labour (*CORE* Ch. 1.9) Specialization increases labour productivity through three mechanisms: **(1) Learning by doing** (acquiring skill while producing), **(2) Difference in ability / comparative advantage** (assigning people/regions to what they are relatively best at), and **(3) Economies of scale** (producing a large number of units lowers average cost per unit). Market exchange allows people to specialize in producing one good while consuming many. #### Planetary Limits and the Biosphere (*CORE* Ch. 1.13 & Topic 1 Ex. 4) Rapid growth in GDP per capita since the Industrial Revolution has relied on fossil fuels and resource extraction, creating **climate change**, **biodiversity loss**, and **resource depletion**. - **Earth Overshoot Day (Topic 1 Ex. 4)**: The calendar date on which humanity's annual demand for ecological resources and services exceeds what Earth's ecosystems can regenerate in that entire year (moving from December in 1971 to late July/early August today). - **GDP Ignores Environmental Depletion**: GDP records timber harvesting, oil extraction, and pollution cleanup as positive value creation, without subtracting the degradation of natural capital (*Fall 2023 Part 1 Q2*, *Spring 2025 Part 2 Q3*). --- ## 2. **Innovation / Schumpeterian Rent**: Temporary economic rent earned by a firm that first adopts a cost-reducing new technology before competitors copy it and drive down the market price. ### 2.2 Technology, Dominance, and Isocost Lines #### Production Technologies and Dominance A **technology** is a process that takes a set of inputs (such as labour $L$ and energy/raw materials $R$, or marine diesel $F$ and electricity $E$) and creates a specified quantity of output (e.g., $100\text{ metres}$ of cloth or $1\text{ ferry trip}$). - **Dominated Technology**: Technology $C$ is **dominated** by Technology $B$ if $C$ uses **more of at least one input and no less of any input** than $B$ to produce the exact same output (i.e., $C$ lies **above and/or to the right** of $B$ in input space). - **Dominance Elimination Rule**: A cost-minimizing firm will **never** choose a dominated technology under any positive input prices $(w > 0, p > 0)$. #### Isocost Lines: Derivation, Slope, and Intercepts (Lecture 3 & Whiteboard 3) When several technologies are **undominated** (one uses more labour/diesel while another uses more capital/electricity), the firm's choice depends on **relative input prices**. Let $L$ be the input on the **horizontal axis** with price $w$, and let $R$ be the input on the **vertical axis** with price $p$. The **total cost** of employing bundle $(L, R)$ is: $$C = w \cdot L + p \cdot R$$ An **isocost line** is the locus of all input combinations $(L, R)$ that cost the exact same total amount $C$. Solving for the vertical-axis variable $R$ gives the linear equation: $$R = \underbrace{\frac{C}{p}}_{\text{Vertical intercept}} - \underbrace{\left(\frac{w}{p}\right)}_{\text{Absolute slope}} L$$ - **Slope of the Isocost Line**: $$\text{Slope} = -\frac{w}{p} = -\frac{\text{Price of horizontal-axis input}}{\text{Price of vertical-axis input}}$$ The absolute value $\frac{w}{p}$ is the **relative price of input $L$ in terms of input $R$** (how many units of $R$ you can buy for the price of $1$ unit of $L$). - **Intercepts**: - **Vertical intercept ($L = 0$)**: $R_{\max} = \frac{C}{p}$ (how many units of $R$ can be bought if all $C$ is spent on $R$). - **Horizontal intercept ($R = 0$)**: $L_{\max} = \frac{C}{w}$ (how many units of $L$ can be bought if all $C$ is spent on $L$). - **Ranking Isocost Lines**: Holding prices $(w, p)$ fixed, all isocost lines are **parallel** (same slope $-w/p$). Isocost lines **closer to the origin** represent **lower total cost $C$**. Therefore, to minimize cost, the firm selects the technology that lies on the **lowest (innermost) isocost line**. --- #### Worked Exam Example: Studying vs. Working (*Spring 2025 Part 2 Q1* & *Fall 2025 Part 1 Q2*) - **Setup**: Studying for 3 hours gives a benefit of $1,000\text{ NOK}$ and has a disutility (effort cost) of $300\text{ NOK}$. 300 = \mathbf{700\text{ NOK}}$. 2. **Opportunity cost of studying (net value of reservation option $B$, working)**: $600 - 200 = \mathbf{400\text{ NOK}}$. 3. **Economic cost of studying**: $\text{Direct cost } (300) + \text{Opportunity cost } (400) = \mathbf{700\text{ NOK}}$. 4. **Economic rent from studying**: $$\text{Economic Rent} = \text{Net Value}(A) - \text{Opportunity Cost}(A) = 700 - 400 = \mathbf{300\text{ NOK}} > 0$$ 5. **Interpretation**: Because the economic rent is strictly positive ($+300\text{ NOK}$), you should choose to **study**. *(In Fall 2025 Part 1 Q2, for studying to yield a positive economic gain, its net value must exceed the $400\text{ NOK}$ opportunity cost.)* --- ### 2.3 Relative Price Changes, Carbon Taxes, and Creative Destruction #### Worked Flagship Problem: *Fjordfrakt* $\text{CO}_2$ Tax & Technology Switch (Lecture 4 Problem) The freight company *Fjordfrakt* can operate a ferry route using four alternative technologies combining **marine diesel ($F$, tonnes, horizontal axis)** and **electricity ($E$, MWh, vertical axis)**: - Topic 3: Optimal Choices — Scarcity, Wellbeing, and Working Hours **Course Alignment**: *CORE Microeconomics 2.0* Ch. 3.1–3.9 *(Fig. 3.13b & Fig. 3.16 skipped)* | **Lectures 5–7** (Whiteboard 6, Lecture 7 Problem) | **Exercises Topic 3 Set A & Set B** ### 3.1 Preferences, Indifference Curves, and the Marginal Rate of Substitution ($MRS$) An individual chooses between two goods that both contribute to wellbeing (**utility** $U$): - **Free time ($t$, horizontal axis)**: Hours per day not spent in paid work ($t = 24 - h$, where $h$ is working hours). - **Consumption ($c$, vertical axis)**: Daily spending on goods and services (in NOK or USD). #### Properties of Indifference Curves (Lecture 5 & Whiteboard 6) An **indifference curve (IC)** joins all combinations $(t, c)$ that provide the exact same level of utility $U(t, c) = \bar{U}$. Standard indifference curves have four properties: 1. **Downward-sloping**: If both $t$ and $c$ are "goods" (more is preferred to less), gaining $1\text{ hour}$ of free time must be offset by giving up some consumption $\Delta c < 0$ to keep utility constant. 2. **Higher indifference curves represent higher utility**: Moving up and to the right increases both $t$ and $c$ ($U_3 > U_2 > U_1$). 3. **Indifference curves never cross**: If two ICs crossed, the intersection point would have the same utility as two points where one strictly dominates the other (violating transitivity). 4. **Smooth and bowed inward (convex to the origin)**: As you move to the right along an indifference curve (more free time $t$, less consumption $c$), the curve becomes **flatter**. #### The Marginal Rate of Substitution ($MRS$) The **Marginal Rate of Substitution ($MRS$)** is the maximum amount of consumption $c$ a person is willing to give up to obtain **one additional hour of free time $t$** while remaining on the same indifference curve: $$MRS(t, c) = \left|\text{Slope of the indifference curve}\right| = -\left.\frac{\Delta c}{\Delta t}\right|_{U = \bar{U}} = \frac{MU_t}{MU_c}$$ - **Diminishing $MRS$**: When free time $t$ is scarce and consumption $c$ is abundant (top-left of an IC), the individual values an extra hour of free time highly ($MRS$ is large, curve is steep). When free time is abundant and consumption is scarce (bottom-right of an IC), the individual is only willing to give up a few kroner for another hour of free time ($MRS$ is small, curve is flat). - **Calculating $MRS$ from a Table (Topic 3 Set A Ex. 3 & Spring 2025 Part 1 Q4)**: Given combinations on the same indifference curve: $E(15\text{h}, 540)$, $F(16\text{h}, 450)$, $G(18\text{h}, 323)$, $H(19\text{h}, 282)$, $D(20\text{h}, 250)$: - Between $G(18, 323)$ and $H(19, 282)$: $MRS = |282 - 323| = \mathbf{41}$ (willing to give up $41$ units of consumption for the 19th hour of free time). - Between $H(19, 282)$ and $D(20, 250)$: $MRS = |250 - 282| = \mathbf{32}$ (diminishing $MRS$: $32 < 41$). - **Special Case — When Free Time Becomes a "Bad" (Topic 3 Set A Ex. 3e)**: If having more than $20\text{ hours}$ of free time causes boredom so the worker requires *more* consumption to compensate for forced extra free time, the indifference curve **slopes upward** for $t > 20$. --- ### 3.2 The Feasible Frontier and Optimal Choice ($MRS = MRT$) #### Budget Constraint, Feasible Set, and Marginal Rate of Transformation ($MRT$) Suppose a worker earns an hourly wage $w$ (in NOK/hour), works $h = 24 - t$ hours per day, and has non-labour income $m$ (such as an unconditional cash transfer or pension; $m = 0$ if wage is the only income). The **budget constraint (feasible frontier)** is: $$c = w(24 - t) + m = (24w + m) - w \cdot t$$ - **Feasible Set**: All bundles $(t, c)$ satisfying $c \le w(24 - t) + m$ and $0 \le t \le 24$. - **Marginal Rate of Transformation ($MRT$)**: The quantity of consumption the worker *must* sacrifice in the marketplace to gain one additional hour of free time. It equals the **absolute slope of the budget constraint**, which is the **hourly wage $w$** (the opportunity cost of $1\text{ hour}$ of free time): $$MRT = \left|\frac{dc}{dt}\right| = w$$ #### Constrained Optimization Rule ($MRS = MRT$) (Lecture 6 & Lecture 7 Problem Parts A–B) To maximize utility subject to the budget constraint, the worker chooses the point on the budget line that reaches the **highest possible indifference curve**—the point of **tangency**: $$\text{Optimal Interior Choice } E^*: \quad MRS(t^*, c^*) = MRT = w$$ | Position on Budget Line | Slope Comparison | Economic Meaning & Optimal Adjustment | | :--- | :--- | :--- | | **Left of $E^*$ (e.g., Point B: $t=12, c=3000$)** | $MRS > MRT$ *(IC is steeper than budget line)* | Worker is willing to give up *more* consumption for $1\text{h}$ of free time than the market requires ($w$). **Action: Work less / take more free time ($t \uparrow, c \downarrow$)** toward $E^*$. | | **At Tangency $E^*$ (e.g., $t^*=16, c^*=2000$)** | $MRS = MRT = w$ *(IC is tangent to budget line)* | Subjective valuation of $1\text{h}$ of free time equals its market opportunity cost $w$. **Action: Utility is maximized ($h^* = 8\text{h}$ work).** | | **Right of $E^*$ (e.g., Point D: $t=20, c=1000$)** | $MRS < MRT$ *(IC is flatter than budget line)* | Worker values $1\text{h}$ of free time at *less* than the wage $w$ they could earn by working that hour. **Action: Work more / take less free time ($t \downarrow, c \uparrow$)** toward $E^*$. | --- ### 3.3 Income and Substitution Effects of Wage and Tax Changes When the hourly wage $w$ increases (e.g., from $w_1 = 250\text{ NOK/h}$ to $w_2 = 500\text{ NOK/h}$ in Lecture 7 Problem 1, or when the income tax rate is cut), the budget constraint **pivots outward around the horizontal intercept $(t=24, c=0)$** and becomes **steeper** ($MRT$ rises from $250$ to $500$). An employment contract transfers **temporary authority** over the worker's activities, not ownership of the person. #### Separation of Ownership and Control (*Fall 2024 Part 2 Q1* & *Spring 2025 Part 2 Q2*) In modern corporations, **owners (shareholders)** are the residual claimants who receive profits, while **managers** and **employees** run day-to-day operations. This creates a **Principal–Agent Problem** between **Owners (Principal) $\leftrightarrow$ Managers (Agent)** and between **Managers (Principal) $\leftrightarrow$ Workers (Agent)** due to two conditions: 1. **Conflict of Interest**: Owners want to maximize firm profits, whereas managers/workers may prefer high salaries, perks, empire-building, or low work effort. 2. **Asymmetric Information & Unverifiability**: Owners/managers cannot perfectly observe or verify in court how hard managers or employees work. **Why Employment Contracts Are Incomplete (*CORE* Ch. 6.4)**: 1. The firm cannot foresee every future contingency or task at the time of hiring. 2. Observing and measuring individual work effort accurately is costly or impossible. 3. Even if a manager observes low effort, **effort is not verifiable in a court of law**—so a piece-rate or complete contract enforcing exact effort cannot be written for most modern jobs. **How Owners Align Managerial Incentives (*Fall 2024 Part 2 Q1*)**: 1. **Performance-related pay** (bonuses, shares, or stock options tied to firm share price/profits). 2. **Monitoring by the Board of Directors** backed by the threat of **dismissal**. --- ### 4.2 Employment Rent and the Cost of Job Loss Because managers cannot enforce effort via a complete contract, they motivate workers by paying an **efficiency wage** $w$ high enough that the worker earns an **economic rent from keeping the job**—called **employment rent** (the **cost of job loss**). remaining weeks after firing $= h - s = 75\text{ weeks}$). - $w$: Weekly (or hourly) wage paid by the firm. - $c$: Weekly (or hourly) cost/disutility of effort saved by shirking. - $w_r$: Weekly (or hourly) **reservation wage**—the net payoff the worker receives per week after being fired during the remaining $h - s$ weeks. #### Derivation of the No-Shirking Condition ($\text{Area B} \ge \text{Area A}$) 1. **Total Payoff from Working Hard for $h$ Weeks**: $$V_{\text{work}} = h(w - c)$$ 2. **Total Payoff from Shirking** (collects full wage $w$ with zero effort cost for $s$ weeks, then gets fired and receives $w_r$ for $h - s$ weeks): $$V_{\text{shirk}} = s \cdot w + (h - s)w_r$$ 3. **No-Shirking Condition ($V_{\text{work}} \ge V_{\text{shirk}}$)**: $$h(w - c) \ge sw + (h - s)w_r \iff (s + h - s)(w - c) \ge sw + (h - s)w_r$$ Rearranging terms to compare the two shaded rectangles in Figure 4.1b: $$\underbrace{(w - c - w_r)(h - s)}_{\text{Area B: Employment rent lost after week } s} \ge \underbrace{c \cdot s}_{\text{Area A: Effort cost saved during weeks } 0 \dots s}$$ 4. **Solving for the Minimum No-Shirking Wage ($w^{NS}$)**: $$w^{NS} = w_r + c + \left(\frac{s}{h - s}\right) c$$ #### Worked Example: *Jonas at Solsiden* (Lecture 11 Problem 1 Q3) - **Given**: $w_r = 8,000\text{ NOK/wk}$, $c = 1,500\text{ NOK/wk}$, $h = 100\text{ weeks}$, caught after $s = 25\text{ weeks}$ ($h - s = 75\text{ weeks}$). - **No-Shirking Wage**: $$w^{NS} = 8,000 + 1,500 + \left(\frac{25}{100 - 25}\right) \times 1,500 = 9,500 + \frac{1}{3}(1,500) = \mathbf{10,000\text{ NOK/week}}$$ - **Area Check**: $\text{Area A} = 1,500 \times 25 = \mathbf{37,500\text{ NOK}}$; Topic 5: Supply, Demand, and Competitive Markets **Course Alignment**: *CORE Microeconomics 2.0* Ch. 8.1–8.6, 8.8, 8.10 | **Lectures 9–11** (Whiteboard 9, Whiteboard 10, Lecture 11 Problem 2) | **Exercises Topic 5 Set A & Set B** ### 5.1 Demand (Willingness to Pay) and Supply (Marginal Cost) #### The Market Demand Curve (Buyers' Willingness to Pay) Each potential buyer has a **Willingness to Pay (WTP)** (reservation price)—the maximum price at which they will buy a unit of the good. Ordering all buyers from **highest WTP to lowest WTP** forms the **downward-sloping market demand curve $D$**: - At any market price $P$, all consumers with $\text{WTP} \ge P$ buy the good; consumers with $\text{WTP} < P$ do not buy (*Fall 2023 Part 1 Q7*). #### The Price-Taking Firm & Market Supply Curve (*Fall 2024 Part 2 Q3* & *V2026 Part 3a*) In a competitive market with many buyers and many sellers of an identical product, each individual firm is a **price-taker**: it cannot influence the market price $P$ (if it sets a price above $P$, it loses all customers; if it sells below $P$, it sacrifices profit unnecessarily). - **Marginal Cost ($MC$)**: The additional cost of producing one more unit of output ($MC = \frac{\Delta C}{\Delta Q}$). In the short run with fixed capacity (e.g., bakery ovens), $MC$ slopes **upward** as output increases because producing extra units requires overtime pay, crowding equipment, or less efficient inputs. - **Profit-Maximization Rule for a Price-Taking Firm ($P = MC$)**: - If $P > MC(Q)$, producing one more unit adds $P$ to revenue and only $MC$ to cost, increasing profit by $P - MC > 0 \implies$ **expand output**. - If $P < MC(Q)$, the last unit costs more to produce than it sells for $\implies$ **reduce output**. - Therefore, a price-taking firm maximizes profit by producing the quantity where: $$\text{Price} = \text{Marginal Cost} \iff P = MC(Q)$$ - Consequently, **a competitive firm's marginal cost curve IS its individual supply curve**, and the **market supply curve $S$** is the horizontal sum of all firms' marginal cost curves (ordering units from lowest seller reservation price/$MC$ to highest). --- ### 5.2 Price-Taking Firms, Market Equilibrium, and Surplus #### Market-Clearing Equilibrium ($Q^D(P^*) = Q^S(P^*)$) At the **competitive equilibrium $(Q^*, P^*)$**, the quantity demanded equals the quantity supplied (**market clearing**): - **If $P > P^*$ (Excess Supply / Surplus)**: $Q^S(P) > Q^D(P)$. Some sellers cannot find buyers; competing sellers cut prices toward $P^*$ to offload unsold inventory. - **If $P < P^*$ (Excess Demand / Shortage)**: $Q^D(P) > Q^S(P)$ (*Spring 2025 Part 1 Q8*). Frustrated buyers are willing to pay more than $P$, so buyers/sellers bid the price up toward $P^*$—unless prevented by a binding **price ceiling** $\hat{P} < P^*$ (Topic 5 Set A Ex. 1e), which creates a persistent shortage $Q^D(\hat{P}) - Q^S(\hat{P})$. - **Two Empirical Tests for Perfect Competition (*CORE* Ch. 8.10 & Lecture 10)**: 1. **Law of One Price**: Do all transactions take place at the same market-clearing price $P^*$? 2. **Marginal Cost Pricing ($P = MC$)**: Are firms selling at a price equal to marginal cost (rather than charging a markup $P > MC$)? #### Consumer Surplus ($CS$), Producer Surplus ($PS$), and Deadweight Loss ($DWL$) Every trade at $P^*$ generates gains from trade: - **Consumer Surplus ($CS$)**: Sum of $(\text{WTP}_i - P^*)$ across all units bought $=$ **area below the demand curve and above the horizontal price line $P^*$**. - **Producer Surplus ($PS$)**: Sum of $(P^* - MC_i)$ across all units sold $=$ **area above the supply ($MC$) curve and below the horizontal price line $P^*$**. *(Note: $PS$ equals variable revenue minus variable cost; short-run profit equals $PS - \text{Fixed Costs}$).* - **Total Surplus ($TS$) & Pareto Efficiency**: $$TS = CS + PS$$ At the competitive equilibrium $Q^*$, **Total Surplus is maximized** and **Deadweight Loss ($DWL$) is zero**—every unit with $\text{WTP} \ge MC$ is traded, and no unit with $\text{WTP} < MC$ is produced (**Pareto efficient**). - **Efficiency vs. Fairness (Lecture 10 & Whiteboard 10)**: Pareto efficiency only means the total pie $TS$ is as large as possible; it says nothing about whether the distribution of surplus is fair. The side of the market with the **steeper (less elastic)** curve captures the **larger share of total surplus**. - **Worked Calculation: *Bread Market in Trondheim* (Lecture 11 Problem 2)**: - Demand intercept $P_{\max}^D = 70\text{ NOK}$, Supply intercept $P_{\min}^S = 10\text{ NOK}$, Equilibrium $Q^* = 10,000\text{ loaves/day}$ at $P^* = 30\text{ NOK}$ (50 bakeries $\implies q^* = 200\text{ loaves/bakery}$): $$\begin{aligned} CS &= \frac{1}{2} \times 10,000 \times (70 - 30) = \mathbf{200,000\text{ NOK/day}} \\ PS &= \frac{1}{2} \times 10,000 \times (30 - 10) = \mathbf{100,000\text{ NOK/day}} \\ TS &= CS + PS = \mathbf{300,000\text{ NOK/day}} \end{aligned}$$ --- ### 5.3 Comparative Statics: Curve Shifts, Steepness, and Tariffs #### Movements Along vs. Shifts of Supply and Demand (*Fall 2025 Part 1 Q8*) - A change in the good's **own price $P$** causes a **movement along** the curve, **never** a shift. - **Demand Shifts Right (Up)** when: **(1)** consumer income rises (for a normal good), **(2)** the price of a **substitute** rises (e.g., higher electricity price increases demand for solar panels, *Fall 2025 Q8*), **(3)** the price of a **complement** falls, **(4)** tastes/preferences shift toward the good, or **(5)** the number of buyers increases. - **Supply Shifts Right (Down)** when: **(1)** technology improves (lowering $MC$), **(2)** input prices (wages, energy, raw materials) fall, **(3)** taxes/tariffs are lowered, or **(4)** new firms enter the industry. | Exogenous Shock | Curve That Shifts | Equilibrium Price $P^*$ | Equilibrium Quantity $Q^*$ | Direction of $P^*$ and $Q^*$ | | :--- | :--- | :---: | :---: | :--- | | **Positive Demand Shock** *(e.g., holiday nut demand)* | $D$ shifts **right/up** | $P^* \uparrow$ | $Q^* \uparrow$ | Move in the **same** direction | | **Negative Demand Shock** | $D$ shifts **left/down** | $P^* \downarrow$ | $Q^* \downarrow$ | Move in the **same** direction | | **Positive Supply Shock** *(e.g., better baking ovens)* | $S$ shifts **right/down** ($MC \downarrow$) | $P^* \downarrow$ | $Q^* \uparrow$ | Move in **opposite** directions | | **Negative Supply Shock / Tariff** *(e.g., $+15\%$ tariff)* | $S$ shifts **left/up** ($MC \uparrow$) | $P^* \uparrow$ | $Q^* \downarrow$ | Move in **opposite** directions | #### Worked Exam Problem: *15% Import Tariff on Canned Tomatoes* (*V2026 Exam Part 3* & *Topic 5 Set B Ex. 1–2*) - **Pre-tariff equilibrium $E_0$**: $P_0 = 80\text{ USD per thousand cans}$, $Q_0 = 100$. The **Labour Force ($L$)** is represented as a vertical line (inelastic supply of workers). - **Diagram Axes**: - **Horizontal axis**: Aggregate **Employment ($N$)** (number of employed workers or $\%$ of working-age population). **Unemployment ($u$)** is read from **right to left** as the horizontal distance between the **vertical Labour Force line** and **Employment $N$**. - **Vertical axis**: **Real wage ($w = W/P$)**, bounded above by the horizontal dashed line at **Output per worker ($\lambda$)**. #### 1. The Wage-Setting (WS) Curve (Upward-Sloping) - **Definition**: Shows the minimum real wage $w^{WS}(N)$ required at each level of aggregate employment $N$ to provide workers with sufficient employment rent to work hard rather than shirk. - **Why the WS Curve Slopes Upward (*Fall 2024 Part 3b*, *Spring 2025 Part 3b*, *Fall 2025 Part 3b*)**: As aggregate employment $N$ increases (moving right), the **unemployment rate $u$ falls**. When unemployment is low, a fired worker can find a new job much more quickly (**expected unemployment duration falls**). This **raises the worker's reservation wage $w_r$** and **reduces the cost of job loss (employment rent)** at the existing wage. To restore discipline and prevent shirking, HR departments across the economy must offer a **higher real wage $w$**. #### 2. The Price-Setting (PS) Curve (Horizontal) - **Definition**: Shows the real wage $w^{PS}$ that results when firms set prices $P$ as a profit-maximizing markup over marginal/unit labour cost $MC = \frac{W}{\lambda}$. - **Division of Output per Worker ($\lambda$)**: Each employed worker produces $\lambda$ units of real output, which is split between the **real wage paid to the worker ($w$)** and **real profit per worker going to owners ($\lambda - w$)**: $$\lambda = \underbrace{w}_{\text{Real wage per worker}} + \underbrace{(\lambda - w)}_{\text{Real profit per worker}} \iff w^{PS} = \frac{W}{P} = \lambda(1 - \sigma)$$ where $\sigma = \frac{\lambda - w}{\lambda}$ is the **profit share** of output (determined by firms' market power / profit markup) and $1 - \sigma = \frac{w}{\lambda}$ is the **wage share** of output. #### 3. Nash Equilibrium in the Labour Market ($A: w^{WS}(N^*) = w^{PS}$) - **Structural (Equilibrium) Unemployment ($u^* > 0$)**: Equilibrium occurs at **Point A** $(N^*, w^*)$ where the WS and PS curves intersect. - **Why Equilibrium Unemployment Can Never Be Zero**: If unemployment were zero ($N = L$), a fired worker could walk across the street and get an identical job immediately ($u_{\text{wks}} = 0 \implies \text{Employment Rent} = 0$). No finite wage could prevent shirking, so the WS curve shoots up toward infinity before reaching the Labour Force line and always intersects PS to the left of $L$. - **Why Firms Don't Cut Wages Below $w^*$ When Unemployment Exists (*Fall 2024 Part 3c*)**: Although unemployed workers would accept a job below $w^*$, cutting the wage below the WS curve would cause existing workers to shirk, lowering productivity and reducing firm profits. --- ### 6.3 Comparative Statics: Shifts in the WS and PS Curves > [!tip] Methodological Note: Why Curves Shift (*Spring 2025 Exam Part 3e*) > A curve in an economic diagram plots the relationship between two **endogenous** variables (here, Employment $N$ and Real Wage $w$) under a ***ceteris paribus*** ("all else equal") assumption holding background (**exogenous**) variables fixed. \quad G = 1 \implies \text{one person gets } 100\% \text{ of income})$$ - **Market Income vs. Disposable Income**: Direct progressive taxes and cash transfers cause the Lorenz curve for **disposable income** to lie **closer to the $45^\circ$ line** than the Lorenz curve for **market income** ($G_{\text{disposable}} < G_{\text{market}}$). - **Advantage of Lorenz Curve over Gini (Lecture 13 Slide 14)**: Two societies can have the exact same Gini ratio for completely different structural reasons (e.g., a large group of unemployed with $0$ income vs. a tiny group of super-rich capital owners); When nominal wages rise above the PS curve, firms' profit margins are squeezed below $\sigma$. Firms respond by **raising prices $P$** ("eaten up by inflation") and reducing employment. In the new equilibrium, the **real wage is unchanged ($w^* = w^{PS}$)** while **structural unemployment is higher ($N^{ff} < N^*$)**. 2. **The Union Voice (Motivation / Workers' Response) Effect (Lecture 13 Slide 23)**: - When unions give employees a respected voice in workplace organization and foster constructive cooperation with management, work feels less onerous (**disutility of effort $c$ falls**) $\implies$ **shifts the WS curve DOWNWARD** to $WS_{\text{voice}}$, **increasing equilibrium employment ($N^{ff+} > N^*$)**. (If cooperation also raises labour productivity $\lambda$, the PS curve shifts up as well!) #### The Norwegian Model of Wage Formation (*Frontfagsmodellen*) (Lecture 13 Slide 24, Canvas Podcast & *Fall 2025 Part 3c–d*) - **Institutional Architecture**: Norway combines high union density ($\sim 50\%$) and collective bargaining coverage ($\sim 70\%$) across four main employee confederations (**LO, Unio, YS, Akademikerne**) and employer organizations (**NHO, Virke, Spekter, KS**), supported by common macroeconomic facts from **TBU** (*Det tekniske beregningsutvalget*) and mediation by **Riksmekleren**. - **How Pattern Bargaining (*Frontfagsmodellen*) Works**: 1. Annual wage negotiations start in the **internationally exposed / export-competing manufacturing sector (*frontfaget*)**—specifically between *Fellesforbundet* (LO) and *Norsk Industri* (NHO). 2. Unlike sheltered domestic firms or the public sector, export-competing firms are **international price-takers**: they cannot pass excessive nominal wage increases onto foreign customers through higher prices without losing market share and going bankrupt. 3. The wage growth frame (*rammen*) agreed in the *frontfag* acts as a **binding norm** (neither a floor nor a ceiling in a single year, but a target norm over time) for all subsequent negotiations in the sheltered private sector and the public sector. - **How to Illustrate *Frontfagsmodellen* in the WS–PS Diagram (*Fall 2025 Exam Part 3c–d*)**: - Coordinated unions internalize the macroeconomic costs of excessive wage claims (loss of international competitiveness, inflation, and unemployment) and exercise **wage restraint**. - Graphically, coordinated bargaining **shifts the WS curve DOWNWARD** relative to uncoordinated bargaining. - **Main Macroeconomic Result**: Because the equilibrium real wage $w^*$ is pinned down by the horizontal PS curve, coordinated wage bargaining does **not** directly produce a higher real wage; instead, its triumph is achieving **higher equilibrium employment $N^*$ and permanently lower structural unemployment $u^*$**! --- ## 8. Business Cycle (*CORE* Ch. 3.9–3.10) Because of **diminishing marginal returns to consumption** at any single date, households prefer a smooth consumption trajectory over time (**borrowing when young**, **saving and repaying debt during middle-aged peak earning years**, and **drawing down savings in retirement**): - **Response to a Temporary Income Shock** (*Fall 2025 Part 1 Q10*): Households keep consumption nearly flat by **self-insuring** (drawing down savings or borrowing) and **co-insuring** (family networks, unemployment insurance, progressive tax-and-transfer system). - **Response to a Permanent Income Shock** (*Melting Glacier*, Topic 8 Ex. 3b): When a forward-looking tour guide learns at date $t_1$ that the glacier will permanently melt at date $t_2$ (halving after $t_2$. #### Three Limits to Consumption Smoothing (*CORE* Ch. 3.10 & Topic 8 Ex. 3c) 1. **Credit Constraints (Credit Market Exclusion)**: Poorer households without wealth/collateral cannot borrow when income temporarily dips or when expecting higher future income; their consumption is forced to track current income. 2. **Present Bias / Weakness of Will (Impatience)**: Even when a household knows future income will fall and *can* save (no credit constraint requires borrowing to save!), present bias causes them to delay adjustment until $t_2$, consuming $100$ until the glacier *V2026 Q5*) While households stabilize $C$, firms can easily postpone new machinery or buildings. Investment fluctuates sharply due to **changing expectations about future demand and profits ("animal spirits")** and a **coordination game** across firms: - **Vicious Circle (Low-Investment Nash Equilibrium)**: If Firm A expects weak demand and low capacity utilization, it does not invest; because neither Firm A nor Firm B invests, economy-wide demand and incomes stay low, validating their pessimism. - **Virtuous Circle (High-Investment Nash Equilibrium)**: If firms simultaneously expect strong demand and invest in new capacity, their spending creates jobs and demand across the economy, validating their optimism. --- ## 9. Topic 9: Inflation, CPI, and Conflicting Claims **Course Alignment**: *CORE Macroeconomics 2.0* Ch. 4.1–4.4 | **Upcoming November 2026 Lectures (Lectures 16–17)** | **Exercises Topic 9** ### 9.1 Inflation, Deflation, Disinflation, and the CPI #### Core Price-Level Definitions (*CORE* Ch. 4.1–4.2) - **Inflation ($\pi_t$)**: The annual percentage increase in the general price level of the economy. - **Deflation ($\pi_t < 0$)**: A decrease in the general price level (negative inflation rate; $\text{CPI}_t < \text{CPI}_{t-1}$). - **Disinflation**: A **decrease in the rate of inflation** (e.g., inflation slows from $5.3\%$ to $2.5\%$—prices are still rising, just less rapidly). #### Consumer Price Index (CPI) vs. GDP Deflator - **Consumer Price Index (CPI)**: Measures the cost of a fixed, representative **"shopping basket"** of goods and services bought by an average household, weighted by household budget shares. - **Includes imports** bought by consumers (e.g., imported cars, coffee); **excludes exports** and capital/government goods; **includes VAT/excise taxes**. - **Base Year ($\text{CPI}_{\text{base}} = 100$)**: $$\text{CPI}_t = \frac{\text{Cost of basket in year } t}{\text{Cost of basket in base year}} \times 100, \qquad \pi_t = \frac{\text{CPI}_t - \text{CPI}_{t-1}}{\text{CPI}_{t-1}} \times 100\%$$ - **GDP Deflator**: Ratio of Nominal GDP to Real GDP ($\times 100$). Measures prices of **domestically produced** output (**includes exports, excludes imports**). #### Current vs. Constant Prices & Worked SSB Table (Topic 9 Ex. 1) The relationship between nominal consumption ($\text{Current}_t$) and real consumption in constant base-year prices ($\text{Constant}_t$) is: $$\text{Constant}_t = \frac{\text{Current}_t}{\text{CPI}_t} \times 100 \iff \text{CPI}_t = \frac{\text{Current}_t}{\text{Constant}_t} \times 100$$ *(Syllabus note from `Exercises solutions Topic 9.pdf`: You are not required to memorize the Current/Constant conversion formula on the exam, but you **are** required to know how to calculate $\pi_t$ from $\text{CPI}_t$ and interpret the graph!)* - **Key Graphical Insights from Topic 9 Ex. 1a–c (SSB Data 2010–2022, Base Year 2015)**: - **1a) Identifying the Base Year**: **2015** is the base year because that is where the Current-price and Constant-price curves **intersect** ($1,281,716\text{ mill. NOK} \implies \text{CPI}_{2015} = 100$). - **1b) Why Constant $<$ Current after 2015**: Because the price level in all years after 2015 was higher than in 2015 ($\text{CPI}_t > 100$). - **1c) Trap Question**: Does $\text{Constant}_t < \text{Current}_t$ for all years after 2015 prove that inflation was positive in *every single year* after 2015? **No!** Even if a single year had mild deflation ($\pi_t < 0$), the constant-price curve would still lie below the current-price curve as long as the cumulative price level stayed above the 2015 level ($\text{CPI}_t > 100$). - **Representative Rows from Topic 9 Ex. 1d–e & Ex. 4d**: - **2015**: $\text{Current} = 1,281,716$, $\text{Constant} = 1,281,716 \implies \text{CPI}_{2015} = \mathbf{100.0}$. - **2021**: $\text{Current} = 1,534,999$, $\text{Constant} = 1,338,304 \implies \text{CPI}_{2021} = \mathbf{114.70}$ ($115$). - **2022**: $\text{Current} = 1,712,018$, $\text{Constant} = 1,417,023 \implies \text{CPI}_{2022} = \mathbf{120.82}$ ($121$); $\pi_{2022} = \frac{120.82 - 114.70}{114.70} \times 100\% = \mathbf{5.3\%}$. - **Real Wage Growth Identity (Topic 9 Ex. 4d)**: $\pi_t \approx \%\Delta W_t - \%\Delta w_t$. In 2023, nominal wages grew $5.2\%$ while real wages changed by $-0.1\% \implies \pi_{2023} = 5.2\% - (-0.1\%) = \mathbf{5.3\%}$. --- ### 9.2 Economic Consequences of Inflation and Deflation | Phenomenon | Distributional & Efficiency Effects (*CORE* Ch. 4.3) | | :--- | :--- | | **Unanticipated High Inflation ($\pi \uparrow$)** | - **Net Borrowers (Debtors) WIN / Net Lenders (Creditors/Savers) LOSE**: Loans are fixed in nominal currency, so inflation erodes the **real value of debt**.
- **Fixed-Nominal-Income Earners LOSE**: Workers/pensioners whose pay adjusts slowly suffer real purchasing-power losses.
- **Efficiency Costs**: Blurs **relative price signals** (hard to tell scarcity from general inflation), creates investment uncertainty, **menu costs** (updating prices), and **shoe-leather costs**. | | **Deflation ($\pi < 0$)** | - **Households Postpone Consumption**: Expecting lower prices tomorrow, consumers delay buying durables (cars, housing), collapsing aggregate demand.
- **Rising Real Debt Burden**: Real value of nominal debt rises, triggering household/firm defaults and banking crises.
- **Zero Lower Bound (ZLB)**: Nominal interest rates cannot easily fall below $0\%$. | | **Low, Stable Inflation ($\sim 2\%$ Target)** | - **"Greases the wheels" of the labour market**: Because workers resist nominal wage cuts, $2\%$ inflation lets real wages ($W/P$) adjust downward smoothly in declining sectors without cutting $W$, while keeping a safe buffer above deflation. | --- ### 9.3 Conflicting Claims, the Wage–Price Spiral, and the Phillips Curve In *CORE Macroeconomics 2.0* Ch. 4.4, **Topic 9 Exercise 2**, **Spring 2025 Part 1 Q10**, and **V2026 Exam Part 2 Q3**, inflation and deflation arise directly from **conflicting claims on output per worker ($\lambda$)** in the WS–PS model: - Workers/unions claim a real wage given by the WS curve: $w^{WS}(N)$. - Firms claim a profit share $\sigma$, leaving a price-setting real wage: $w^{PS} = \lambda(1 - \sigma)$. - **The Bargaining Gap**: $$\text{Bargaining Gap}(N) = \frac{w^{WS}(N) - w^{PS}}{w^{PS}}$$ | Labour Market Regime | Position Relative to $N^*$ | Bargaining Gap & Claims | Dynamic Wage–Price Mechanism & Inflation Outcome | | :--- | :---: | :--- | :--- | | **1.
